title: Mean Cross-Entropy Loss
description:
Implement the **mean categorical cross-entropy**. You are given `probs`, a list of `n` rows where row `i` holds the predicted class probabilities for sample `i` (each row sums to 1), and `labels`, a list of `n` integers where `labels[i]` is the correct class index for sample `i`.

The loss for one sample is `-ln(p)` where `p` is the probability assigned to the correct class. Before taking the log, **clip** `p` into the range `[1e-12, 1 - 1e-12]` so that a probability of exactly 0 does not produce infinity. Return the average loss over all samples.

examples.explanation: The correct class has probability 1, so the loss is -ln(1) = 0 (clipping to 1 - 1e-12 changes nothing visible).
The model gave the true class probability 0. Clipping to 1e-12 yields -ln(1e-12) = 27.631 instead of infinity.

hints: Only one probability per row matters: the one at index labels[i].
ln(0) is -infinity. Clamp the picked probability with min(max(p, 1e-12), 1 - 1e-12) first.
Sum -ln(p_i) over rows and divide by the number of rows.
signature: def crossEntropy(self, probs: List[List[float]], labels: List[int]) -> float:
approach:
**Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the true class, averaged over samples.** With a one-hot target only one term of the general sum `-sum_c y_c ln p_c` survives, so per sample we simply look up `probs[i][labels[i]]`, take `-ln`, and average.

The numerical pitfall is `ln(0) = -inf`: one confidently wrong prediction would make the mean infinite and break gradients. Clipping the probability to `[eps, 1 - eps]` bounds the per-sample loss at about 27.6 for `eps = 1e-12`. In real frameworks the loss is computed from logits with log-softmax instead of clipping, which is both more stable and more accurate.

**Interview follow-ups:** Why combine softmax and cross-entropy into one op? (the gradient simplifies to `p - y`, and log-softmax avoids the clip). What changes for binary cross-entropy? (`-(y ln p + (1-y) ln(1-p))`, both branches need clipping). What is label smoothing and how does it change this function? (targets become `(1 - a) * one_hot + a / C`, so every class contributes). How do you weight classes for imbalance?
